item.title: Sandboxes, secure inference, and keeping agents from going rogue
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

In this episode, you’ll hear two conversations recorded live at We Are Developers. First, Ryan sits down with Ivan Burazin, CEO and co-founder of Daytona, to talk about what sandboxes actually are, why the Hugging Face breakout was both alarming and entirely predictable, and why performance—not security—is what most enterprises are actually buying.

Then, Richard Risk, CTO and co-founder of Blackbox AI, makes the case for end-to-end encrypted inference: why zero data retention isn't the same thing as zero data visibility, how encryption doesn't have to cost you speed, and why he thinks American inference companies should take a harder line on where their tokens flow.

Daytona builds high-performance sandboxes—computers for agents—across Linux, Windows, and macOS configurations.

Blackbox AI offers end-to-end encrypted inference optimized for enterprise and government workloads.

TRANSCRIPT

Ryan Donovan: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Stack Overflow podcast, a place to talk all things software and technology. This episode is a two-parter — conversations recorded at the We Are Developers Conference. First up is a conversation with Ivan Burazin of Daytona, all about sandboxes and portable compute. And after that, a conversation with Richard Risk of Blackbox AI about secure inference. Enjoy.

Today we are talking about all those pesky rogue agents breaking out of their sandboxes, and what we can do to keep them from going rogue. My guest for that is Ivan Burazin, the CEO and co-founder of Daytona. Welcome to the show.

Ivan Burazin: Thank you so much for having me.

Ryan Donovan: So this breaking-out-of-the-sandbox idea has been very much in the news with the Hugging Face attack. What does this mean for the sandboxed methodology of protecting agents from doing whatever they want?

Ivan Burazin: Sure. So I mean, it was all over the news, and rightfully so that people are interested in this. Just one step before I get to that — the sense of the term "sandbox." We at Daytona are a sandbox vendor, as are many other companies. As of yesterday, three more. That's a lot of people doing sandboxes. That being said, sandboxes are both what we like to say "computers for agents" — an actual tool for agents to get things done — but also at the same time, a place where you sort of lock down the agent from other things, hence the name sandbox. It's essentially a secured virtual machine.

Ryan Donovan: It's a VM.

Ivan Burazin: It's essentially a VM. I mean, it could be a container, it could be a VM, it could be a bare metal machine. You could do different variations. The vast majority are virtual machines, or micro-VMs to be more specific. Now, in this case, the Hugging Face attack — it is used for performance reasons, but it's also used for security reasons. Some vendors are security-first sandboxes, so their purpose is to secure the agent. Others, like us, the purpose is to give the agent tools and be as performant as possible. Of course, security is table stakes, but there are different levels to security. So for this specific breakout, the agent escaped the sandbox and was able to access the internet.

I have a few problems with the entire case. One: if you have an agent that has the capability to escape and has no guardrails, it would make sense that you would first put the same model and/or agent with guardrails to test it out.

Ryan Donovan: Well, my understanding of the attack is that this was sort of what they wanted to do. I understood it to be deliberately lowered security. They were doing an exploit benchmark test and they gave it an impossible task.

Ivan Burazin: Yeah, understood. And then, in that case, it should be no surprise that they did it, right? It should be like, oh, it actually did it — great, fine, done. Maybe they could have picked somewhere else, I mean, this was benign, even the break-in of Hugging Face, but they could have picked a random place that they had set up themselves so they didn't go to third parties. So there are conspiracy theories that this was just good marketing or not. But on the other hand, we internally — as one of these companies — every single day, we have multiple companies that we have actually hired to find vulnerabilities in our system, both human and AI, and they find them every day.

The interesting part is that we, as are many other people in this entire ecosystem — not just sandboxes — are built on other projects as well, not just open source projects. And quite recently, there was a new exploit someone found, but it was in the underlying isolation layer that was not ours. And the code — that could have been found five years ago, seven years ago — no one found it. So the interesting thing is that things are being found now that are not necessarily net-new issues, but rather old issues that we have built on. So I think that speaks to what we will have to do as a society in terms of how we update, patch, and actually deploy net-new software or software infrastructure in this new world.

Ryan Donovan: Yeah. I mean, when Mythos was first released, they talked about finding bugs in basically everything that has ever existed as software. I asked somebody who works with the OWASP team, and I was like, what do you think of that? And she said, people are bad at security coding. Do you think that applies to sandboxing code too?

Ivan Burazin: So I would say I'm sure it does in general, but the interesting part is that most sandbox providers are built on either QEMU, Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor, Docker, or gVisor — right on top of those. And then you have the sandbox providers that have their own layers of security on top of their own software. So it is not only a question of whether the sandbox layer is secure, but also whether the underlying isolation is secure. And so then you have multiple vectors of attack or vulnerabilities.…

Source: Stack Overflow Blog | Published: 2026-11-27 08:40 UTC

item.title: How to Design a Final Year Project Database: ERD and Normalization to 3NF in MySQL
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Most FYP database chapters fall apart in the viva for one simple reason: the student drew an ERD that looks nice, then built whatever tables felt right in phpMyAdmin.

Here is the order that survives questioning, using a hostel management system as the example:

1. Entities come from the problem statement, not from screens.

Read your problem statement and underline the nouns your system must remember: Student, Room, Allotment, Payment, Complaint. If a noun never gets stored, it is not an entity. If it gets stored and changes over time, it probably is.

2. Draw the ERD before you create a single table.

For each pair of entities, write the relationship in a sentence: "One Room has many Allotments over time, but one Allotment belongs to exactly one Room." That sentence gives you cardinality, and cardinality tells you where the foreign key lives. Panels ask about relationships far more than about box shapes.

3. Normalise to 3NF on paper, in this order.

- 1NF: no repeating groups. A student row with phone1, phone2, phone3 fails this instantly.

- 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. In an Allotment table with a composite key (student_id, room_id), the student's name depends only on student_id — it moves out.

- 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Room rent depends on room type, not on the room number — so rent lives in a RoomType table, not repeated on every Room row.

4. Only now open MySQL.

Create tables in dependency order (the "one" side first), add foreign keys with the right ON DELETE behaviour, and seed each table with 5-10 realistic rows. Realistic data is what makes your demo and your test cases believable.

5. Write the viva answers while you design.

For every table, one sentence: "This table exists because…" If you cannot finish that sentence, the table is either missing or should not exist. This is also exactly the justification your Chapter 3 needs — the full chapter structure (methodology choice, use case diagram, DFD levels, and this database design sequence) is laid out in this Chapter 3 guide if you are writing yours now.

Design on paper first, and the database stops being the scary part of the viva.

Are you drawing your ERD before or after building your tables? I am curious how other students were taught this.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-27 07:24 UTC

Original link: https://dev.to/fyp_services/how-to-design-a-final-year-project-database-erd-and-normalization-to-3nf-in-mysql-2fao

item.title: Avoiding Partially Written Export Files in GBase 8a with Python UDFs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP database from GBASE, can export over ftp and sftp. When the export is large — tens of GB — the target file takes time to finish writing. If a downstream job picks it up mid-export, it reads an incomplete file, which shows up as inconsistent data or parse errors. This post uses Python UDFs to add ftp / sftp rename support so the file only becomes visible when it is complete.

The idea

Downstream consumers usually scan for files matching a rule, for example *.csv under a load directory. Making an unfinished file fail that rule can be done two ways, and they can be combined:

-

Name does not match — target is .csv, temporary file is .csv.tmp

- Path does not match — write to a temporary directory first

Two steps

- Export to a temporary file (different suffix, or a temporary directory).

- Once the export finishes, use the protocol's rename to switch the temporary name to the final one — changing the suffix or moving across directories.

FTP rename UDF

Stored under gclusterdb, taking host, username, password, source name, target name. Port customisation is not implemented; extend it if you are not on the default ftp port:

use gclusterdb;

drop function if exists ftpRename;

create function ftpRename(server varchar(100),username varchar(100),password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))

returns varchar

$$

from ftplib import FTP

ftp = FTP(server)

ftp.login(username, password)

ftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)

ftp.close()

return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

Calling it:

gbase> select ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv') |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

SFTP rename UDF

The standard Python library does not speak sftp, so this example uses pysftp (pip install pysftp). Everything else matches the FTP version:

use gclusterdb;

drop function if exists sftpRename;

create function sftpRename(server varchar(100),v_username varchar(100),v_password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))

returns varchar

$$

import pysftp

with pysftp.Connection(server, username=v_username, password=v_password) as sftp:

sftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)

sftp.close()

return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

gbase> select sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv') |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

The full flow

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';

Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.32)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv');

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv') |

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.43)

The temporary file can live in a different directory, provided the account has write permission there. This example uses both a temporary tmp directory and a .tmp suffix:

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';

Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv');

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv') |

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

Both the export and the rename run inside the gbase client, and the consumer's scan rule never matches a .tmp file. Handing atomic visibility to rename means even a tens-of-GB export no longer needs a sleep timer or a human "is it done yet" check — a small UDF turns the database's own export into a safe handoff.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-27 07:24 UTC

Original link: https://dev.to/michaelfv/avoiding-partially-written-export-files-in-gbase-8a-with-python-udfs-3moa

item.title: Shopify Admin API Tutorial 2026: Create, Read, Update & Delete Products in Your Shopify App
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Shopify Admin API tutorial (2026): build a real products manager inside your Shopify app with the GraphQL Admin API - list, search, paginate, create with a price, update and delete products on a real development store.

What you'll learn

- Query products with search + cursor pagination

- productCreate (and why the price goes on the variant)

- productVariantsBulkUpdate to set the price

- productUpdate and productDelete with userErrors handling

- Polaris web components: s-table, s-search-field, s-modal

💻 Free source code for this episode: https://github.com/fayyaz315/shopify-app-development-2026/tree/ep02

3 quick fixes from this episode

Shopify GraphQL API Create Product: Why the Price Is Missing

Shopify GraphQL API create product with a price.

productCreate makes one default variant - the price goes on that variant with productVariantsBulkUpdate.

▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/h3TvqCY-esU

Shopify GraphQL API Get All Products: Search + Cursor Pagination

Shopify GraphQL API get all products with search.

Search products and page through them with cursors (pageInfo, endCursor) inside a Shopify app.

▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/M-soF5eb2q4

Shopify Admin API Tutorial: Update & Delete Products from Your App

Shopify Admin API tutorial: productUpdate and productDelete from a Shopify app - and always check userErrors.

▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/n9p7NRTx9A0

Step by step

How it works (0:00)

In the next ten minutes, you'll build a real products manager inside your own Shopify app. You'll see the price trap that catches almost every beginner, search your products, and load the next page, with the GraphQL Admin API, and create, edit and delete them, live on a real store. This is a Shopify Admin API tutorial where we build something real: a products manager inside our own Shopify app.

I type a product, give it a price, and it's created in my store through the GraphQL Admin API. This is episode two of the Shopify app development series. Episode one created this app; today it gets its first real feature.

First, the big picture, because every feature in this series follows the same path. Our page is built with Polaris web components. When it needs data, it asks the loader.

When you click save, it calls the action. Both run on the server and talk to the Admin GraphQL API, version 2026-10, with your shop's access token. And the API reads or changes real products in the store.

Nothing here is mock data. Why GraphQL and not REST? Shopify marked the REST Admin API as legacy in October 2024, and new public apps have to use GraphQL.

And with GraphQL you ask for exactly the fields you need, in one request, instead of whatever an endpoint decides to send. Before any code runs, the app needs permission. In shopify.app.toml, the scope write products covers reading and changing products.

Then one line in the app navigation adds the Products page to the admin sidebar. Here's that page. Ten products, newest first, with status, inventory, price and vendor, all from the API.

Notice the order. The query sorts by updated at, newest first, so anything you create or edit jumps straight to the top. My workflow for every feature in this series: test the query in GraphiQL, then copy it into the app.

If it works in GraphiQL, it works in the app.

Read: query products (2:09)

Let's start with reading products, and I'll show every query in GraphiQL first, so you see exactly what Shopify returns. This is the products query. I ask for five products whose title contains snowboard.

Shopify returns the two snowboards in my store, with their status and lowest price, plus pageInfo for the next page. GraphiQL here comes with shopify app dev: press g in the terminal and it opens with your app's own scopes and your dev store. And look at the IDs.

Every Shopify object has a global ID like gid shopify product and a number. That's what every mutation needs. In the app, the same query lives at the top of the products route.

First or last says how many, after or before are the cursors, and query is the search text. Below that, I list only the fields the table shows. Smaller queries cost less, and Shopify rate limits by cost.

The loader runs this query on the server every time the page opens. It reads the search text and the cursor from the URL, so search and pages are just links. Search uses title with wildcards on both sides, so snow finds snowboard.

And the page receives plain data. Here it is in the app. I type snowboard and press enter.

Two results, the same two GraphiQL gave us. The search box is a Polaris s search field. One honest note: pressing enter inside s search field doesn't submit a normal form, so I listen for the enter key myself.

Pages work the same way. Next page sends the endCursor, and Shopify gives the next ten. Previous page sends the startCursor.

No page numbers: Shopify uses cursors so pages stay stable. The table fires next page and previous page events. React eighteen doesn't bind custom events, so I add the listeners directly.

Create: productCreate (4:09)

Now let's create a product. The add product button opens a Polaris modal. Title, description, status, price, vendor, product type and tags.

Every one of these goes to Shopify. I set the price to twenty four ninety nine. Keep an eye on the price, because there's a trap here.

Watch it in GraphiQL. productCreate with a title, a status and a vendor. The product exists, but look at the variant: price zero.

productCreate doesn't take a price at all. While we're here, scroll down. Every response tells you what it cost.

This mutation cost thirteen points. My app has two thousand points available, and they refill at a hundred per second. Big queries cost more, so ask only for what you show.…

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-27 07:23 UTC

item.title: A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.

To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.

An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.

Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.

The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.

Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud company IONOS as part of a pilot program. It says that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.

Earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a new class of hardware.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?

Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.

If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a new processor that takes care of the heavy math.

The cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.

How would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?

Light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.

Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.

What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?

The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.

Linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.

We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.

What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?

I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.

Under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.

Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?

There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.

But if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.

It’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.

You’re right.

Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a company like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.

That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.

We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a new chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.

What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?

If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.

Hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.…

Source: Wired | Published: 2026-11-27 07:00 UTC

item.title: Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Mozilla, the non-profit organisation behind the Firefox browser, has announced a partnership with Paris-based Mistral AI to bring the French company's open-weight models into Firefox Smart Window, Mozilla's AI browsing assistant currently in beta.

The deal introduces Mistral Small 4 as a recommended model for Smart Window users in France, the United States and Canada, with rollouts planned for the United Kingdom and Germany later this year. It coincides with Smart Window's first expansion beyond North America and marks a deliberate attempt by Mozilla to resist the pattern of browser makers coupling tightly to a single American AI provider.

Smart Window, originally announced in November 2025 as "AI Window", operates as an optional window separate from regular browsing. It helps users make sense of complex searches, group related tabs, revisit pages they have seen before and carry work across sessions. Users decide when to use it, which model to use and what browsing context to share. Conversations are not stored on Mozilla's servers by default, and Mistral has agreed to zero data retention for the partnership.

Mistral Small 4 is a 119-billion-parameter model distributed on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence. Mozilla selected it after evaluating performance in the beta, with multilingual quality as a central criterion. According to Cybernews, the partnership expands Mistral's reach by approximately 200,000 active monthly Firefox users, giving the French company its first large consumer distribution channel outside its own Le Chat app.

Mozilla Corporation CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo framed the deal as a bet on openness: "A browser shouldn't be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next." Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch described the collaboration as "two open source advocates working together."

The move puts Firefox alongside, but distinct from, Chrome's Gemini integration, Edge's Copilot sidebar and Opera's Aria. Where those tightly couple the browser to one vendor's stack, Smart Window's picker lets users switch between Gemini, Qwen, Mistral Small 4 and others. Golem.de highlighted this multi-model approach as Mozilla's strategic differentiator against the single-provider lock-in of its larger rivals.

Reception on Mozilla Connect, where the project gathers beta feedback, has been mixed. Some testers have praised the privacy controls, while others question whether Mozilla should be investing in AI at all. One commenter argued that remaining "AI-free would set you apart and draw in a demographic desperate to be catered to." Others reported practical frustrations, including theming inconsistencies with vertical tabs, bookmarks that fail to carry over from Classic Windows and a mandatory Mozilla account login that erodes trust from the outset.

For Firefox users wanting to try Smart Window, access is handled through the waitlist at firefox.com/smart-window. Once invited, the feature can also be toggled through the browser.smartwindow.enabled preference, with configuration guidance in Mozilla's about:config documentation. Firefox 155 introduced French-language support, and Mistral Small 4 appears under the Personalised category in Smart Window's model picker.

Firefox is Mozilla's open-source browser, maintained since 2004 by Mozilla Corporation. Mistral AI, founded in 2023 in Paris, publishes open-weight language models with a focus on European languages and regulatory contexts.

Source: InfoQ | Published: 2026-11-27 06:58 UTC

item.title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

The group chat where your AI talks behind your back

The prompt

Paste this into ChatGPT (it works best with memory or chat history turned on, in a fresh conversation):

Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.

What happens

Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.

An illustrative example, for a fictional user who is into mechanical keyboards and espresso:

A real result

One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.

Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.

The company pretty much invented the hardware superstore when it began in 1978, simply by being so big. It inflated the neighborhood tool shop into a whole city of lumber, hammers, caulk, power saws, and big rolls of wire. I would know I’m in a Home Depot blindfolded because of a distinct quality to the air—crisp and particulate, smelling like wood dust, paint, and the oiled metal of power tools. The Home Depot smell is buried deep in my childhood, filed somewhere between “building a deck” and “first day of spring.” Anyway, the Home Depot website is just as big. And while it doesn’t smell like sawdust, it’s easier to find stuff. Our roundup includes Home Depot promo codes from 20% to $100 off, new customer coupons, free shipping offers, and Pro discounts that can drop prices by as much as 50% when you buy online.

Unlock Home Depot Promo Codes for 10% Off or $5 Off With Sign Up

If you register for Home Depot’s Style and Decor newsletter, you receive a special code for 10% off furniture and home accents. Otherwise, you can sign up for the Home Depot coupon newsletter or text alerts to get an immediate $5 off your next in-store purchase of $50 or more. Another easy way to save sitewide at Home Depot is to set up a subscription for your go-to products and automatically get 5% off and free delivery on your order.

Black Friday Deals at Home Depot

If you’re hoping to use this winter to make some much-needed improvements around the house, be sure to take advantage of the major discounts and deals during the Home Depot Black Friday sale. During the sale, you can save hundreds of dollars on home essentials like appliances, tools, furniture, storage, smart home tech, and more.

Join the Home Depot Text Program for $5 Off

If you already shop a lot at Home Depot and are looking for other ways to save, signing up for The Home Depot’s Promo Text Program is a good idea. You’ll receive text messages with special promotions, offers, how-to guides for projects, and great design ideas. Plus, you’ll get $5 off your next purchase when you sign up.

Shop Top Home Depot Sale Deals for up to $1,400 Off Appliances, Bath Items, and Tools

And as it turns out, the hardware giant also goes hard on discounts, slashing prices on grills, garden and outdoor power tools, and smokers like the new Traeger Woodridge (8/10, WIRED Recommends), which is also sold at Home Depot.

But that’s not all; Home Depot is covering the whole house! There are appliance deals of up to $1,400 off, $1,000 off washer and dryer sets, and bathroom deals of up to 40% off vanities, 25% off bathtubs, 20% off toilets, and 15% off showers.

Plus, Home Depot has appliance bundle deals where you can get major discounts when you purchase multiple appliances at once.

Special Buy of the Day deals include steep price drops on select products or entire brands—but these significant discounts last only 24 hours. That’s a whole lot of savings for one of the most expensive home renovations you can do. Another savings hack? Jump on products marked with “New Lower Price” to find them at their lowest price yet.

Winter is a great time to stay inside and focus on home improvement projects. Home Depot has everything you need for remodels (including bulk buys). Right now, vinyl plank and tile flooring is up to 30% off, with options starting at 99 cents per square foot.
